explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The text says Satan is standing at Joshua's right hand "…to accuse him." (Zechariah 3:1). He didn't show up for small talk. Joshua is the high priest, and Satan is right there at his side, ready to point a finger.

A blessing would be a lovely surprise, baker, but that's not why Satan is there. The text says he stands at Joshua's right hand "…to accuse him." (Zechariah 3:1). Satan showing up with a blessing would be like a smoke alarm showing up with a gift basket.

I get the thought, baker. Joshua is the high priest, so a crown could sound like it fits. But the text says Satan stands at his right hand "…to accuse him." (Zechariah 3:1). Nobody is handing out crowns in this scene yet.

That's it, baker. The LORD says, "The LORD rebukes you, Satan!" (Zechariah 3:2). Satan is there to accuse, and the LORD is the one who speaks up. Then He asks, "Is not this man a firebrand snatched from the fire?" (Zechariah 3:2).

explanations.answer: You may test him for a time
explanations.explanation: That line sounds like another story, baker. In Job, God does let Satan test Job (Job 1:12). Here in Zechariah, the LORD says something very different: "The LORD rebukes you, Satan!" (Zechariah 3:2). No testing is offered, and the accuser gets shut down.
Good guess, baker, because Satan is there to accuse. But the LORD doesn't say anything like that. He says, "The LORD rebukes you, Satan!" (Zechariah 3:2). The rebuke is His whole answer to Satan.

Not quite, baker. The text says, "Now Joshua was dressed in filthy garments as he stood before the angel." (Zechariah 3:3). This high priest is standing there in a mess. Fine priestly robes are not what he has on.

Right, baker. The text says Joshua "…was dressed in filthy garments…" as he stood before the angel (Zechariah 3:3). That's a rough outfit for a high priest. I've worn dust and drawer lint myself, so I'm not judging.

You've got it, baker. The angel says to those standing before him, "Take off his filthy clothes!" (Zechariah 3:4). Joshua doesn't have to scrub himself clean. Somebody else takes the dirty clothes off him.

explanations.answer: Send him out of the camp
explanations.explanation: I see why that might come to mind, baker, but nobody is being sent anywhere. The angel says, "Take off his filthy clothes!" (Zechariah 3:4). Joshua isn't getting thrown out. He's getting taken care of.

explanations.answer: Let him wash in the river
explanations.explanation: Washing makes sense with filthy clothes, baker. But the text never mentions a river or any washing. The angel simply says, "Take off his filthy clothes!" (Zechariah 3:4). The cleanup comes from others, not from Joshua himself.
That's the one, baker. The angel tells Joshua, "See, I have removed your iniquity…" (Zechariah 3:4). Iniquity means sin, and it's gone. It was lifted off Joshua, not earned back by him.
Joshua's health is never the topic, baker. The angel tells him, "See, I have removed your iniquity…" (Zechariah 3:4). Iniquity means sin. That's the thing that got taken away.

That would be a kind thing to remove, baker. But the text says something else. The angel tells Joshua, "See, I have removed your iniquity…" (Zechariah 3:4). Iniquity is sin, and that's what was removed.
Yes, baker. The angel says, "…I will clothe you with splendid robes." (Zechariah 3:4). Filthy clothes come off and something splendid goes on. That's a big upgrade.

This one is true, baker. The angel tells Joshua, "…I will clothe you with splendid robes." (Zechariah 3:4). It's a promise, not a maybe. The filthy clothes don't just come off and leave him standing there.

Right, baker. Zechariah says, "Let them put a clean turban on his head." (Zechariah 3:5). Then a clean turban was placed on Joshua's head. He's been wearing filthy garments, so clean is exactly the word.

Golden sounds fancy, baker, but that's not the word. Zechariah says, "Let them put a clean turban on his head." (Zechariah 3:5). Nothing about gold. After those filthy garments, clean is the whole point.
I can see the thinking, baker. A high priest and a turban do sound pretty royal. But Zechariah asks for "…a clean turban…" (Zechariah 3:5). He never says royal.

explanations.answer: Walk in His ways and keep His instructions
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The angel of the LORD gives Joshua a charge from the LORD of Hosts: "If you walk in My ways and keep My instructions…" (Zechariah 3:7). Notice that this comes right after Joshua's clothes are changed. That's a big job, and I'm glad it came after the new robes.

explanations.answer: Rebuild the wall around all of Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Wall building is a real job, baker, but it's not this charge. The angel of the LORD gives Joshua a charge from the LORD of Hosts: "If you walk in My ways and keep My instructions…" (Zechariah 3:7). It's about how Joshua lives, not a construction project.

explanations.answer: Offer a lamb on the altar every morning
explanations.explanation: Joshua is a priest, so I see why you'd go there, baker. But this charge doesn't mention a lamb or an altar. The angel of the LORD gives Joshua a charge from the LORD of Hosts: "If you walk in My ways and keep My instructions…" (Zechariah 3:7).

Yes, baker. The LORD of Hosts says, "…I will give you a place among these who are standing here." (Zechariah 3:7). Joshua started this scene with an accuser at his side. Now he's promised a spot among those standing there.

This one is true, baker. The LORD of Hosts says, "…I will give you a place among these who are standing here." (Zechariah 3:7). Joshua started with an accuser beside him. Now a place is promised to him.

Right, baker. The LORD of Hosts says, "…I will remove the iniquity of this land in a single day." (Zechariah 3:9). Joshua's iniquity was already removed in verse 4. Now the promise gets bigger, from one man to the whole land.

This one is true, baker. The LORD of Hosts says, "…I will remove the iniquity of this land in a single day." (Zechariah 3:9). Joshua's iniquity was removed in verse 4. Then the promise grows to cover the whole land.

explanations.answer: Sit under your own vine and fig tree
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The LORD of Hosts says, "…you will each invite your neighbor to sit under your own vine and fig tree." (Zechariah 3:10). Picture neighbors waving each other over to sit down. I like this picture a lot.

explanations.answer: Stand guard with you on the city wall
explanations.explanation: A wall guard is serious business, baker, but that's not the invitation. The LORD of Hosts says, "…you will each invite your neighbor to sit under your own vine and fig tree." (Zechariah 3:10). Sitting, not standing watch.

explanations.answer: Help you rebuild the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Helping with a building project sounds like a good neighborly thing, baker, but it's not what this verse says. The LORD of Hosts says, "…you will each invite your neighbor to sit under your own vine and fig tree." (Zechariah 3:10). The invitation is to sit down, not to start working.
